[00:00] Avery Chen: hey everyone thanks for making time, i'm avery from redwood, i'll kick us off. can you hear me ok?
[00:06] Markus Lindholm: yeah loud and clear, thanks. quick intro from nimbus, i'm markus, cto, priya runs model infra and santiago is infra lead on latency and networking stuff.
[00:15] Avery Chen: great, i'll hand to lina to do a short run of the optimize console and the mixed-precision profile flow. lina?
[00:20] Lina Patel: hey all, hi, let me share screen. so high level this is the optimize tab, we have prebuilt qprofiles, int8-first, fp8-hybrid, and a mixed rollout helper that will produce a canary plan across versions. want to start with the int8 vs fp8 fidelity matrix.
[00:34] Priya Rao: quick Q, our main concern is summarization of clinical notes, hallucination is a big no. We're running Llama-3-70B variant on prem. is there prior work on hallucination impact when moving to int8?
[00:47] Lina Patel: yep, we do sensitivity runs. int8 tends to be lower latency but you can see small drift on rare token probabilities which for hallucination-y cases matters. that's why the console pairs qprofiles with target prompt sets and automatic evals. we recommend staged rollout with canary splits at 1%/5%/20% while monitoring ROUGE/accuracy and hallucination-specific metrics.
[01:05] [inaudible] Santiago Perez: can you repeat the canary sizes?
[01:08] Lina Patel: sure, 1% then 5% then 20% then full. those are templates, you customize by endpoint.
[01:15] Markus Lindholm: what about mixing fp8 for sensitive routes and int8 for general chit chat routes? we have some endpoints that are lower-stakes.
[01:22] Lina Patel: absolutely, route level policy is supported. you can assign a qprofile per route and set fallback behavior if fidelity drops. so, clinical-summarize route stays on fp8 (or even bf16), while conversational routing uses int8 for throughput.
[01:33] Avery Chen: i want to call out cost/lantency tradeoff. int8 can reduce token cost by roughly 35-45% in our benchmarks, latency per token also drops, but quantization sensitivity depends on model family and prompt distribution.
[01:48] Priya Rao: do you have a published benchmark for l3-70B or similar? int8 numbers are great but we need concrete numbers to justify to compliance.
[01:56] Lina Patel: we have a verified benchmark PDF, i'll share. note: sometimes product names are transcribed wrong in the auto reports, but the raw CSV is the source of truth.
[02:06] Santiago Perez: curious about VPC vs hosted latency, if we go private vpc regionally what's the delta we should expect?
[02:12] Avery Chen: typical delta for private deployment in same region is 5-25ms additional cold start+network overhead, warm paths with gRPC are sub 5ms added for request/response. depends on your network egress setup and KMS calls if you use remote HSM.
[02:26] Markus Lindholm: we use a KMS in a different AZ right now which occasionally adds jitter. any recommendations?
[02:31] Lina Patel: bring KMS closer to the compute or use caching tokens for a short TTL to avoid per-request KMS handshake. Redwood supports HSM/KMS integrations but those calls are async and we log them in audit.
[02:43] [00:03] Lina Patel: ok back to qprofiles, i'll run a quick simulated evaluation, i'm gonna pick three profiles: baseline float32, int8-agg, and fp8-mix.
[02:50] [02:52] Lina Patel: starting eval, note these are lightweight evals inside the console, for full fidelity you run in-customer benchmarks or our benchmark harness.
[03:05] [03:06] System: (screen share) running 1k prompt eval against your supplied set (demo uses a redwood sample set)
[03:12] Priya Rao: that demo prompt set looks more general, ours has a lot of structured medical abbreviations, can that change the sensitivity?
[03:18] Lina Patel: yes, domain tokens and rare subword splits can expose quantization artifacts. that's why we ask for a representative prompt set.
[03:25] [03:28] Lina Patel: quick results coming in... baseline float32 latency median 210ms per response, int8-agg median 150ms, fp8-mix median 165ms. fidelity delta (we run a duplicate-diff metric) shows int8 had a 0.8% ROUGE drop on this sample, fp8-mix 0.2% drop.
[03:50] Markus Lindholm: 0.8% drop on rouge — is that clinically meaningful? we need a threshold. we typically reject anything with more than 0.5% degradation on key metrics.
[03:59] Lina Patel: that's why staged canary with A/B evals is important. if your threshold is 0.5% then maybe start int8 at 1% traffic and monitor fidelity compared to baseline, with auto-rollback if exceeds threshold.
[04:12] Priya Rao: can automatic rollback be tied to specific hallucination detectors? we have a custom checker that flags hallucination patterns.
[04:18] Lina Patel: yes, the console integrates external metrics via webhooks and you can map those to guardrails. if the external metric trips, model variants are automatically shifted per policy. there can be a 30s-60s reaction time depending on your metric reporting frequency.
[04:33] Santiago Perez: any tips about KV cache impact? we rely heavily on long conversations and prefix caching.
[04:39] Lina Patel: if you have KV cache warm paths, quantization tends to have less per-token overhead because the heavy attention compute is amortized; however cold starts and very long context windows can amplify differences. test with representative session lengths.
[04:51] Avery Chen: another point—mixed-precision rollback is supported at token granularity for some model backends, meaning you can use fp8 for initial tokens and switch to int8 for subsequent tokens in low-stakes flows. it's experimental but sometimes helps with fidelity-sensitive prefixes.
[05:06] Priya Rao: that token-granularity switching sounds neat but sounds risky, any examples?
[05:12] Lina Patel: it's used for system prompt-heavy flows: keep sysprompt and initial few tokens in higher precision then drop to int8 for the rest. we expose it as an escape hatch with strong observability.
[05:24] [05:25] Markus Lindholm: ok, let's talk about audit/compliance artifacts — we need reports for SOC2 and an ability to show all canary experiments and rollbacks historically.
[05:34] Avery Chen: console stores rollout history, audit trail, and the qprofile hashes used. for Private deployment we can provide offline export of the audit logs and tie them into your SIEM.
[05:43] Priya Rao: can we run the evaluation harness in our private cluster?
[05:47] Lina Patel: yes, we have a bench harness you can run on prem that reproduces the Optimize eval results; it outputs CSVs, ROC curves, and a fidelity diff. we'll provide the repo and runbook.
[05:58] Santiago Perez: network test — when you say 5-25ms delta for private, is that per-request or per-token?
[06:04] Avery Chen: that's per-request roundtrip overhead. Per-token is dominated by model compute which is unchanged by the VPC mode; quantization affects compute latency.
[06:14] [06:15] Priya Rao: another question: if we pin model versions and then roll qprofiles separately, can we guarantee the same behavior across dedicated pools and private infra?
[06:24] Lina Patel: yes, behavior is consistent — qprofiles are identifiers for kernel selection and op paths; on private we ship the same runtime and kernel selection logic, so you get consistent perf. differences come from hardware (GPU type) and driver versions.
[06:36] Markus Lindholm: any gotchas with mixed quantization on A100 vs H100?
[06:40] Lina Patel: h100 tends to be more stable with fp8 paths; a100 int8 kernels are mature but fp8 may be slower relative to a100 int8 for some op patterns. we recommend microbenchmarks on your target GPU.
[06:53] [07:00] Lina Patel: ok i'm going to sketch a recommended rollout: 1) gather 1k representative prompts; 2) baseline float32 run; 3) run int8 and fp8-mix qprofiles in console harness; 4) pick target route-level thresholds; 5) run canary 1% with auto-eval + webhook to your hallucination detector; 6) ramp 5%/20%/100% with monitoring; 7) tag rollout and snapshot audit logs.
[07:28] Priya Rao: timeline wise, how long for Redwood to support putting this into our private environment and run the bench?
[07:35] Avery Chen: once we get the prompt set and access details, bench harness install and baseline run is typically 3-5 business days, then two days for qprofile runs and analysis — so about one week for an initial report.
[07:47] Markus Lindholm: rough cost delta — if we shift 50% of traffic to int8 what cost saving ballpark do we see?
[07:53] Lina Patel: ballpark savings depend on token distribution, but expect 25-40% on inference compute cost; also the throughput increase can reduce latency-driven autoscaling which multiplies savings. we'll include a cost model in the playbook.
[08:07] [08:10] Santiago Perez: any single point failures we should watch for during rollout? like qprofile mis-application or stale KV caches?
[08:17] Lina Patel: guardrails: 1) automated rollback policies 2) monitoring for fidelity delta 3) tag-based release so you can immediately revert by traffic steering and 4) cache warmers for transitions.
[08:30] Priya Rao: ok sounds reasonable. can you email the playbook and the bench harness repo link?
[08:36] Avery Chen: yes i'll send both, plus a sample qprofile JSON and the recommended threshold template.
[08:42] Markus Lindholm: final — we need to loop in security for KMS/HSM integration review. who should they contact?
[08:48] Avery Chen: i'll cc security, our contact is David Morris in security; i'll add him to the thread.
[08:53] [08:54] Priya Rao: one more small ask — can we get a short doc about token-granularity mixed-precision use cases and risk notes?
[08:59] Lina Patel: yep, we'll attach a short note with examples and telemetry guidance.
